lead: Both readings show a God who comes down to seek us. Hebrews says that the Son shared our flesh and blood so that he might become “a merciful and faithful high priest” and help those who are tested. In Luke a woman lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches for one lost coin, and there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. The key words are shared and found.

r.h: He shared our flesh and blood
set: The first chapters of Hebrews show that the Son is greater than the angels (chapter 1). Then the author faces a question: if the Son is so great, why did he become man and suffer? He answers from Psalm 8: the Son was made “for a little while lower than the angels” so that “by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone” (2:9). Today's verses explain why this was fitting. This is the first time Hebrews calls Jesus “high priest”, the great theme of the letter.
str: vv. 14–15: he shared flesh and blood to destroy the power of death and the devil.
v. 16: he came to help the descendants of Abraham, not angels.
vv. 17–18: like us in every respect, a merciful and faithful high priest who helps those who are tested.
kw: The children “share” flesh and blood; the Son “likewise shared” the same things. The word for fellowship, koinōnia, is in the root. God enters into fellowship with our human condition.
a merciful and faithful high priest
Merciful toward us, faithful toward God. A high priest stands between God and the people. Jesus can do this perfectly because he is both.
to make a sacrifice of atonement
The verb of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies with blood. Hebrews will show that Christ fulfils this once for all with his own blood (9:11–14).
vv: Since, therefore, the children share flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared the same things,
The Incarnation is not a disguise. The Son took a real human nature, body and soul, and lived a real human life.
and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by the fear of death.
Fear of death can rule a whole life. Christ went through death and broke its power, so that his own need not live as slaves of that fear.
Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested.
Jesus knows our trials from within. Hebrews later adds that he was tested in every way as we are, “yet without sin” (4:15).
ch: The Church reads this passage as a key to the Incarnation and the priesthood of Christ. St Gregory of Nazianzus wrote that what was not assumed was not healed (Letter 101, in substance): the Son took all that is human in order to save all that is human. The Catechism teaches that Christ is the one high priest, in whom everything the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured is fulfilled (CCC 1544), and that he conquered the tempter for us, as one able to sympathize with our weaknesses (CCC 540).

r.h: The woman who searches for the lost coin
set: Luke 15 holds three parables of the lost: the sheep, the coin and the son. They answer the grumbling of some Pharisees and scribes who said, “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them” (15:2). The parable of the coin is found only in Luke. It stands between the shepherd and the father, and here the one who searches is a woman.
str: v. 8: one coin lost; lamp, broom and careful search.
v. 9: found; friends and neighbours called to rejoice.
v. 10: so there is joy before the angels over one sinner who repents.
kw: A Greek silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a labourer. For a poor woman ten coins could be all her savings.
Literally “change one's mind”: a turning of the whole person back to God. In the parable the coin does nothing; the woman does all the searching. Repentance is first of all being found.
vv: does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?
Houses of poor families often had few windows and earthen floors. Finding a small coin meant patient, careful work. God searches for us with the same patience.
Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.
Joy is meant to be shared. Heaven's joy over a sinner who returns is a feast to which the whole community is invited.
Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
“In the presence of the angels” is a reverent way of speaking of God himself. It is God who rejoices.
ch: The Church hears in this parable the heart of God who seeks sinners. The Catechism teaches that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom and that he speaks of the boundless mercy of the Father for them and of the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (CCC 545). Some Fathers, among them St Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 34, in substance), saw in the woman the Wisdom of God, and in the lamp the light of God shining in Christ's humanity. The sacrament of Penance is the place where the lost coin is found again.

qa: If Jesus was tested like us, could he have sinned?

The Church teaches that Jesus was truly tempted but was without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His temptations were real, not play-acting, but his will was perfectly united with the Father's. Because he never gave in, he knows the full weight of temptation better than we do, and he can help us in ours.
study: What fear has the strongest grip on my life, and how does the victory of Christ over death speak to it?
Is there someone in my family or parish who is “lost” and whom I could help God to search for?
